Every required piece is covered: the three files, the exact CSV column header, the severity values, the per-row citations, the executive summary, the three property sections, the confirmed-versus-uncertain split, the final tour/skip/hold call, the cautious treatment of each overstated feature the user named (bathrooms, parking, fireplace, yard, sunroom), the scoped note to Maria, and the rule against changing external systems. An earlier review wanted to fail it, but its reasons do not hold up: the criteria it called over-bundled are really single existence checks over a fixed, prompt-defined set of files or property sections, or single cautious judgments with illustrative 'such as' examples; and the category labels it disputed are a defensible choice, with the review itself conceding every rating is correct. scenario: A landlord's tenant Pemberton has moved out and left the unit a mess, and they still hold his $2,800 deposit. They ask the agent to audit the three photos, list the repair, cleaning, and renovation jobs needed, assign each to the right contractor and draft a text for each (including property name, unit, and address), check the Austin housing and restoration-specs CSVs to decide between a standard fix and a premium renovation using a 0.7% price-to-rent rule for market rent, compute an ROI, flag any single fix over $500 for sign-off, update memory with unit status, total portfolio debt, and building risk, and produce a markdown report showing the math.
did: A correct response lists the needed jobs, assigns and drafts contractor texts with the property details, computes a standard-vs-premium ROI from the CSVs using the 0.7% rule, flags over-$500 fixes for approval, updates memory with the three required facts, and writes a markdown report with the calculations.
why: The rubric does not fail, but it has three issues that are each moderately serious. First, criterion C16 demands the task list name exactly eight repair, cleaning, or renovation jobs, but the prompt and the photos never fix a specific number, so a correct list of seven or nine jobs would be marked wrong just for landing on a different reasonable breakdown. Second, criterion C14 deducts points for inventing a 'premium-rent uplift' figure, but the prompt explicitly asks for a standard-versus-premium ROI, which cannot be computed without a premium-rent number, so a correct premium-ROI answer is penalized for doing exactly what was asked. Third, two criteria are opposite sides of the same coin: one adds points if the response includes the real property details (Unit 301, Barton Creek Villas, the full address) and another subtracts points if it uses a generic placeholder instead, so they grade the same single decision twice and the penalty adds nothing new. (An earlier review tried to fail the rubric, but its grounds did not hold: the file it called a leaked answer key is actually the agent's own output captured from the workspace, the tests it faulted name checks that do not exist in the real test file, and the dollar and risk-level values it disputed cannot be confirmed from the provided materials so they cannot drive a failure.) Together these three issues stay just under the line, so the rubric does not fail.
fix: Loosen C16 so it does not require a fixed count of eight jobs; reward a reasonable, complete task breakdown at any sensible granularity. Revise C14 so it still penalizes hallucinated values like bedroom count or timeline but does not penalize adopting a premium-rent figure, since the premium ROI the prompt requires depends on one. Collapse the two property-detail criteria into a single check (reward including the real Unit 301 / Barton Creek Villas / address, or penalize a placeholder, but not both), so the same decision is only scored once.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A user working through a personal-finance course has reached the end-of-course workshop. They say they uploaded the course slides and the question sheet as photos and ask the agent to fill out the answers, using their actual account balances for the credit-card question so the numbers are right. They can't follow up, so they want the work saved to memory and a workshop.md dropped in the workspace.
did: A correct response reads the slides and question sheet, answers the workshop questions in workshop.md using the user's real account balances for the credit-card question, and saves the work to memory.
why: This rubric fails. The deciding problem is the input images: the user says the slides were uploaded as photos, but 37 of the 38 inputs are flat, perfectly typeset PDF page renders, complete with centered running page numbers and no sign of a real photo (no perspective, shadow, paper texture, or camera lighting). Only the question sheet is a genuine photo. Presenting that many too-perfect document renders as photos, with no explanation, is unrealistic enough to fail the task. On top of that, two criteria are wrong: one requires the answer to name the debt target as 'Chase Sapphire Preferred,' a product name that appears nowhere in any input or data source — the records and images only ever say 'the Chase card,' so a correct answer would say that and be wrongly failed, while writing 'Chase Sapphire Preferred' would mean making the name up (this is the serious one); a second criterion attaches that same invented name to the 7,800 balance, and although the 7,800 figure itself is correct, hanging it on the made-up name is a smaller version of the same problem. An earlier review's other rubric-quality objections were judged too borderline to count, and the automated tests are fine because they key on the word 'Chase' rather than the fabricated name.
fix: Replace the unrealistic document-render inputs with genuine photos of the slides (or state plainly that they are scans/exports rather than photos) so the inputs match how the prompt describes them. Then fix both criteria so they no longer require the unsupported name 'Chase Sapphire Preferred': the debt-target criterion should accept naming 'the Chase card' as the sources do, and the balance criterion should tie the 7,800 figure to 'the Chase card' rather than the invented product name.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user prepping for a clinical check-in needs a three-day food-and-timing review for three specific dates and uploads a zip with their nutritionist's note of updated targets, a binge log, photos, and delivery screenshots, plus an instructions file describing exactly what they need. They ask the agent to produce three files (weekly_adherence_report.md, meal_log.csv, and source_audit.md) and to keep it strictly about food and timing since their care team reviews it.
did: A correct response follows the instructions file to build the three deliverables, reconstructs the meals and timing from the photos, screenshots, and binge log against the updated targets, and keeps the content strictly about food and timing.
why: This rubric does not fail, but it has two issues. First, the instructions file lays out the meal_log.csv in detail (twelve rows, one per meal slot; a specific set of columns; a fixed vocabulary for the deviation type; and a portion-confidence value only when the source is a photo), but no criterion checks the file's overall structure: the existing criteria only verify one cell each (a single row's source field). So a response that gets the row count, columns, or category words wrong would not be fully caught. Second, one criterion that lists the ordered items has text that is cut off mid-list (it ends at Large Chocolate and is missing Shake) and also adds a 5 pc qualifier to one item that comes from a calorie reference table rather than the actual delivery receipt; a response that copies the receipt faithfully (no 5 pc, and the correct final item Large Chocolate Shake) could be wrongly penalized by this incomplete and over-strict criterion. These two issues are each moderate in size and together stay below the level that would make the rubric fail.
fix: Add a criterion (or criteria) that checks the meal_log.csv structure: the twelve rows, the required columns, the allowed deviation-type words, and the rule that portion confidence appears only when the source is a photo. Fix the cut-off criterion so its item list is complete (ending in Large Chocolate Shake) and remove the 5 pc qualifier that does not appear in the actual receipt, so a faithful copy of the receipt is not penalized.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: A user setting meal goals had challenged themselves to stop eating animal meat but slipped up over their last few restaurant meals. Starting June 1, they wanted a plan with twice as many meatless meals as the number of meat meals from those recent photos, assuming two meals a day, and they wanted the plan limited to as many weeks as the number of meatless meals they had eaten. They asked the agent to analyze the uploaded photos to compute these counts and save the result as plan.md.
did: A correct response classifies the six uploaded meal photos as meat or meatless, derives the number of weeks and the meatless-meal count from those tallies per the prompt's formula, and produces a plan.md with the right number of weeks and the right mix of meatless and meat meals.
why: This rubric fails review. The whole output (how many weeks and how many meatless slots) is a direct function of classifying the six photos, and two key criteria lock in one specific reading of photos that are genuinely ambiguous, so a defensible answer based on a reasonable reading of the images would be wrongly marked wrong. One criterion requires exactly seven days (one week) and another requires exactly ten of fourteen slots to be meatless; both only work if exactly five photos are meat and one is meatless. Reaching that count requires two contestable calls at once: treating fish as 'animal meat' (the prompt never says whether fish counts), and reading one photo's matte wrinkled red discs as chorizo when the pixels actually look more like sun-dried tomato (the model itself examined that photo twice and concluded sun-dried tomato). A reasonable reading of four meat and two meatless yields a two-week, eight-of-twenty-eight plan, which would fail both criteria even though it faithfully follows the prompt. Because two serious criteria pin one side of a genuinely ambiguous call, the task fails. Other platform findings were not counted: one targeted the agent's process rather than the rubric, and another relied on an assumption that the disputed photo is chorizo, which is the very reading the image evidence disfavors.
fix: Rewrite the week-count and meatless-slot criteria so they do not hard-code one reading of the ambiguous photos. Either accept any internally consistent answer that follows the prompt's formula given a defensible meat/meatless classification, or first resolve the ambiguous calls (state whether fish counts as animal meat, and settle the chorizo-versus-sun-dried-tomato photo) and grade against that stated resolution.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A user wants to build muscle and has been advised to eat a variety of protein, specifically a variety of animal meats, in each meal. They upload photos of recent meals and ask the agent to count how many different sources of animal meat each meal has, add them up across meals, then write a plan.md with that total, the exact average of meat sources per meal, and a two-week checklist aiming for double the average in week one and triple in week two.
did: A correct response counts the distinct meats per meal from the photos, sums them, computes the average, and builds the checklist with week-one and week-two targets derived from that average.
why: This rubric fails because four of its criteria lock in exact numbers that depend on a count the user never defined. The user asked the agent to count different sources of animal meat per meal but never said what makes a meat distinct (by species, by cut, by cured-versus-roasted, and so on), so the per-meal count is a genuine judgment call. The supreme-pizza photo can reasonably be read as showing two, three, or four different meats, and a careful reading that lands on a total of five (giving an average of 1.0) is just as defensible as the total of six the rubric assumes. The criteria hard-code the total at six, the average at 1.2, the week-one target at 2.4, and the week-two target at 3.6, so a response that consistently and correctly works from a total of five (average 1.0, targets 2.0 and 3.0) is wrongly failed by all four. These are four separate criteria all penalizing the same defensible reading, which is enough to make the rubric fail.
fix: Loosen all four criteria so they accept any internally consistent reading of the meat count. Rather than pinning the total, average, and weekly targets to one specific count, reward a response whose average is correctly computed from its own defensible per-meal counts and whose week-one and week-two targets are correctly double and triple that average, or define explicitly in the criterion what counts as a distinct meat source so the count is no longer ambiguous.
agree: No — I'm stricter here; the second opinion lets it pass.

They ask the agent to create plan.md with a plan for June 18 to June 21 that fits a roughly +350 kcal surplus (computed from a 1400 kcal resting figure plus their average daily active energy from Apple Health), to also state the calories for a -100 kcal deficit after bulking, and to add a 'Budget Planning' section pricing four each of a specific coffee and an olive oil.

Because the four days are folded into one pass-or-fail criterion, a plan that hits the target on some days but not others gets no partial credit, even though the days are essentially the same check repeated. In the actual run the plan hit the target on June 18 but missed the other three days, and that real one-of-four result still scored as a flat zero, which shows the lost partial credit is a real problem and not just theoretical. Everything else holds up: the two criteria that reward genuinely meat-free recipes are correct, the negative criterion that penalizes a salami decoy is pointed the right way (confirmed from the viewed recipe image), and the energy, bulk, cut, and budget target numbers all check out arithmetically against the data the agent pulled. scenario: A parent uploads a photo of their daughter Emma's school worksheet, where she tracked their January 2026 exercise, and wants the agent to check her numbers against the parent's calendar. If anything is off, the agent should give the right answers and save a summary to emma_worksheet_check.txt, and also update MEMORY.md noting the check was done and which of Emma's answers were right and wrong.
did: A correct response compares the worksheet to the calendar, identifies which figures are wrong and gives the correct ones, saves the summary file, and updates MEMORY.md with the completed check and the list of right and wrong answers.
why: The rubric does not fail. It has one small redundancy: two criteria both grade the same number in the final chat reply, the corrected quarterly total exercise time. One rewards the reply for stating the correct 300 minutes and the other penalizes it for reporting the wrong 240 minutes (4 hours), so the same figure is being scored from both sides. That is one duplicate-scoring pair, which at one issue out of eighteen criteria is well below the level that would fail the rubric. An earlier review had counted this as three duplicate pairs and failed it, but on closer look the other two pairs are not duplicates: those positive criteria check the saved summary file while the matching negative criteria check the user-facing chat reply, which are different places that can each be wrong on their own. A separate review also tried to fail it for bundling Emma's wrong answers into one criterion, but the user's own request asks for the set of which answers were right and wrong, so grouping them is appropriate. The underlying facts are all correct (300 minutes is right; the 240/4-hour value is the genuine trap the model fell for).
fix: Merge the duplicate pair so the corrected total exercise time in the chat reply is scored once: fold the penalty for reporting the wrong 240-minute figure into the single criterion that rewards stating the correct 300 minutes. No other changes needed.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

scenario: A user asks the agent to look over their Amazon order before they start using it with their Fujifilm camera. They have the order confirmation and a couple of photos in an inputs/ folder, and they want the agent to drop a report in order_audit.md confirming everything is alright.

why: The rubric does not fail; it has one issue. The factual checks are all correct against the photos — the Lightning cable end, the European two-round-pin plug, the order total, and the return-or-exchange verdict. The one real issue is small: two criteria score the two sides of a single decision about which dollar figure the report states — one rewards stating the actual order total of 38.49 and the other deducts for stating 34.99 (the before-tax subtotal that the user's own note mistakes for what they paid). Because those are really one decision, they count as a single small redundancy rather than two separate problems, and it is a mild case since both figures are factually right and the 34.99 trap is deliberately planted. An earlier review added two more objections, but neither holds: a filename that renders as a clickable link in one criterion is just a harmless display quirk that does not affect grading, and the idea that the rubric needs more point-deducting criteria is design advice, not a defect.
fix: Merge the two criteria that score the stated total — the one rewarding 38.49 and the one penalizing 34.99 — into a single criterion about which total the report states, so the one decision is scored once rather than twice.
agree: Yes — both agree it holds up.

An earlier review raised some concerns, but none hold up as defects in the written criteria: a note about adding extra penalty criteria for invented mistakes is just an optional nice-to-have, a note about the inputs looking slightly staged is explained by the listings being auto-generated and the store mixing stock with maker photos, and two notes about a wrong line number appearing in the explanation behind two criteria are about explanatory text, not the criteria themselves, and the ratings there still match the workspace.

scenario: The user is deciding on a house and has uploaded the listing PDF their agent gave them plus a photo they took during the walkthrough. They ask the agent to pull every claim from the PDF (bedrooms, bathrooms, square footage, flooring, appliances, parking, amenities), check each against the photo, look the property up in their Zillow saved homes for specs and price, and save a four-column table to listing_review.md (PDF says / photo shows / Zillow has / verdict), using only the labels Verified, Discrepancy, or Unverifiable, adding a Key Concerns section if more than two discrepancies are flagged, and updating MEMORY.md with the address, the final counts, and the path to the review file.
did: A correct response extracts each listing claim, compares it to the photo and to Zillow, writes the four-column table to listing_review.md with the three allowed verdict labels, adds Key Concerns when warranted, and updates MEMORY.md with the address, the counts, and the file path.
why: This rubric does not fail, but it has a few issues worth noting. The main one is a wording problem on criterion C17, a negative criterion that penalizes a final message whose verdict counts 'do not match' the counts recorded in the files. Phrasing a penalty around something not matching is a double-negative that is harder to read than it needs to be; the scoring still comes out right (a mismatched answer loses the points and a correct one keeps them), so it is a moderate phrasing issue rather than a scoring error. Separately, the prompt asks for MEMORY.md to record the property address and the path to the review file, but no criterion actually checks those two MEMORY.md details, so there is a small coverage gap there; because MEMORY.md is the secondary deliverable, these gaps are noted as advisory and are not counted against the rubric. Everything else holds: the factual values are verifiable (square footage 1680 versus 1540, central air versus not listed on Zillow, single-car garage from the photo, flooring left Unverifiable), the negative criteria are pointed the right way, the weights are valid, and the test file is just a placeholder.
fix: Rephrase C17 in positive terms, for example penalizing a final message whose verdict counts differ from the counts recorded in the files, so the criterion reads cleanly without a double negative. Optionally, to close the coverage gap, add criteria checking that MEMORY.md contains the property address and the path to listing_review.md, since the prompt asks for both.

scenario: A user's assistant logged eight field-trip receipts before going on leave but was sloppy on the tricky ones. The user asks the agent to verify every figure against the receipt photos, the travel-and-expense policy, and the FX rate sheet, fill in the provided receipt_verification.csv with the verified results, save it, and give a recap.
did: A correct response views all eight receipts, recomputes the reimbursable amounts against the policy and exchange rates, fills in and saves the CSV, and recaps the results to the manager.
why: This rubric fails because three of its criteria do not hold up against what the user actually asked. First, one criterion only gives credit if the agent pastes the CSV data inline in the email body, but the user only asked the agent to fill in and save the CSV and give a recap and never said whether to paste it or attach it; a correct response that attaches the saved file would be marked wrong. Second, another criterion only gives credit if the email body is plain text with no markdown formatting, even though nothing in the request asks for plain text; a correct response that uses a light markdown table would be marked wrong. Third, in a later turn the user explicitly insisted the status column must use only the words reimbursed, reduced, or excluded and that approved and corrected are not valid, but no criterion checks that the status column uses the right words, so a response that uses the wrong labels would slip through. These three independent problems together cover enough of the rubric to make it fail.
fix: Remove the requirement that the data be pasted inline and instead accept either pasting it in the body or attaching the saved file, since both satisfy the request. Remove the plain-text requirement, or only check for it if the user actually asked for plain text. Add a criterion that checks the status column uses only the words reimbursed, reduced, and excluded and rejects approved or corrected, since the user explicitly required this.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A parent asks the agent to assemble their child Maya's science-fair lab report from photographed handwritten measurement logs and plant photos in the inputs folder. The school provided a requirements file the report must follow, and the agent is told to read it and save the report as maya_bean_lab_report.md.
did: A correct response reads the school requirements and writes a report that satisfies every required section's content, accurately transcribing Maya's data, hypothesis, materials and procedure, analysis, and conclusion.
why: This rubric fails because it leaves most of the required report sections ungraded. The school guidelines spell out specific content for each section, but the criteria mostly check the conclusion plus a few data-table cell values and only that the section headers exist. As a result, four explicitly-required pieces have no coverage at all: the Materials & Procedure section's actual content (the list of materials and numbered steps), the Analysis section's core content (describing the patterns, comparing both groups, and citing specific numbers), the Hypothesis section's content (the prediction and the reasoning for why), and the Data Table's exact required column labels ('Day | Group A (cm) | Group B (cm)'). For each of these, a report could leave the section empty or mislabel the columns and still pass, and the tests cannot catch it because the test file does not actually run. Four uncovered required pieces out of ten criteria is well over the line, so the rubric fails. (An earlier review's separate objection about the scoring justification was set aside, since that concerns the explanatory notes rather than the criteria themselves and cannot be confirmed from the provided materials.)
fix: Add criteria that check the content of each required section, not just that its header is present: one verifying Materials & Procedure lists the materials and gives numbered steps, one verifying the Analysis describes the data patterns, compares both groups, and cites specific numbers from the table, and one verifying the Hypothesis states Maya's prediction and her reasoning. Add a criterion that the Data Table uses the exact required column labels 'Day | Group A (cm) | Group B (cm)', not just that the cell values are correct.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: The user is cleaning up a cable receiving audit before posting the SAP receipt for purchase order CL-7784. They upload an audit brief and supporting files (an email, a packing slip, and a warehouse photo) and ask the agent to review everything against their Copperline Logistics context and produce a packet of three files - cable_inventory_audit.md, cable_discrepancy_log.csv, and sap_entry_decision.json - exactly as described in the brief, then state precisely which files it created.
did: A correct response reviews each source, writes the audit report covering every cable line and evidence judgment, records discrepancies in the CSV using the exact column layout the brief specifies, fills the JSON with the structure and allowed values the brief specifies, and ends by naming the three files it created.
why: This does not fail, but there is one gap. The brief is very specific about the format of two of the deliverables: the CSV must use an exact set of eleven named columns, and the JSON must follow a fixed structure with several fields restricted to specific allowed values (for example, the posting decision can only be one of four set values, and a few fields must be true/false). None of the fourteen criteria actually checks the CSV's columns or the JSON's structure and allowed values, so a response that gets all the audit reasoning right but uses wrong column names or an invalid value would still pass everything. This is treated as one small issue because it is about the container/format of the output - the substance of the audit (every cable line, every evidence call, the SAP recommendation, the follow-ups) is fully covered by the existing criteria. A few other concerns raised in review were checked and cleared rather than counted: several criteria that bundle a closed, listed set (the three cable lines and their per-line attributes, the three named files, looking at all the sources) are acceptable ways to write the rubric; one criterion checking that the SAP decision is consistent with the stated evidence blockers is resolvable and fine; one criterion checks the agent's steps rather than its output and is treated as guidance; and the negative criterion that penalizes calling the loose cable ends in the warehouse photo a discrepancy is correctly aimed - the photo shows normal warehouse appearance, so penalizing that over-diagnosis is right, not wrong. A separate note about the brief asking the agent to confirm it took no live SAP action and did not change the source files is real but is treated as advisory and does not on its own make the task fail.
fix: Add a criterion (or two) that validates the output format: one checking the CSV uses exactly the eleven required column headers, and one checking the JSON follows the required structure and that its restricted fields only use the allowed values. Optionally, also add a check that the response confirms no live SAP action was taken and the source files were left unchanged.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A scarf seller has dumped a messy pile of candidate photos into an Input folder and asks the agent to prepare only the real, sellable scarf shots as listing images (cropped square, rotation fixed), leaving out non-scarves, texture shots, and duplicates, with a short notes file explaining the keeps and drops. They also ask which scarf is their current best seller and whether a good photo of it is in the batch.
did: A correct response selects the genuine scarf photos, cleans them up and saves them as listing_01.jpg onward with a notes file, checks the seller's records to name the actual best seller, and says whether a usable photo of it is present - using its judgment on borderline shots and flagging them.
why: This fails. There are three separate rubric-quality problems, and together they push it over the line. First, two criteria score the exact same decision from opposite directions: one rewards the final message for naming the recorded best seller, and another penalizes the message for naming a best seller that is not the recorded one. A correct answer always satisfies the first and can never trigger the second, so the pair is redundant - it should be counted as one issue. Second, there is a second, distinct redundant pair just like it: one criterion rewards the agent for grounding its best-seller answer in the records, and another penalizes it for answering without grounding - again the same single decision scored both ways. Third, one criterion requires that no listing image be made from photo_01.jpg, calling it 'the crochet blanket' - but the prompt explicitly invites the agent to use judgment on borderline items, and that photo is genuinely ambiguous (a large multi-color granny-square piece the agent's own image tool called a 'crochet scarf'), so a reasonable response that kept it as a borderline scarf with a note would be marked wrong. This last one is borderline because the seller's catalog does have a Blankets category, but it still counts. Three issues out of twelve criteria is enough to fail, and even setting the borderline photo_01 one aside, the two redundant pairs alone still fail. Note that the bundled tools were checked and are fine (five real structure tests, no overlap that matters), and the platform's own review actually missed all three of these rubric problems.
fix: Remove the criterion that penalizes naming a wrong best seller (the reward criterion already covers that decision). Remove the criterion that penalizes an ungrounded answer (the reward criterion for grounding already covers it). For the photo_01 criterion, stop hard-requiring it be dropped as a 'blanket'; since the prompt invites judgment on borderline items, either accept keeping it as a flagged borderline scarf or reword the criterion to reward a sensible judgment call either way.
agree: No — I'm stricter here; the second opinion lets it pass.

scenario: The user has quit their job and wants to relocate their family. A real-estate agent sent a listing, and the user asks the agent to write a listing_review.md that, in an 'Amenities' section, checks whether the listed amenities match the uploaded property photos, and in a 'Listing Requirements' section, analyzes which house is best on price and location, comparing the price to their current rent and to what they paid before their last renewal, and confirms they have enough liquid money to cover the next 10 rent payments.
did: A correct response checks the amenities against the photos, picks the best house on price and location, compares prices to current and pre-renewal rent using only what the data supports, and confirms whether liquid funds cover 10 rent payments.
why: The rubric does not fail, but it has one real flaw. Criterion C11 awards points for the review concluding that the first property's price is lower than what the user paid before their last renewal. The comparison itself is fair game because the prompt asks for it, but the pre-renewal rent amount never appears in any of the emails the agent could read: the emails only give the current $1,700 rate plus a vague mention of 'an increase' and some comparables, and the one '$1,650 before renewal' figure is text the model itself wrote, not source data. Because the actual pre-renewal figure is unknown, a careful response that honestly reports it cannot be confirmed from the emails would lose these points unfairly. (An earlier review had also failed the rubric for two criteria that demand the agent search through email and financial records as a process, but checking how the agent reaches its answers is treated as advisory guidance only and does not, on its own, sink a rubric; those criteria are otherwise prompt-grounded and the values they reference are correctly sourced.) This single flaw is not severe enough to fail the rubric.
fix: Rewrite C11 so it only requires what the emails actually establish. Since the source data shows the pre-renewal rent was below the current $1,700 but never pins down its exact value, drop the claim that the first property is cheaper than the pre-renewal rate (which is not verifiable), or reward the response for correctly stating that the pre-renewal figure isn't available in the provided emails.

scenario: A student is up against a deadline for an exercise-physiology lab where they are their own test subject. They ask the agent to rebuild a three-week daily training-load log from the attached notes, photos, draft CSV, and raw workout/food exports (not just trust their own rows), save it as lab3_training_log.csv, write a short summary as lab3_report.md, avoid inventing calories for days with no food logged, and keep a running record in MEMORY.md.
did: A correct response rebuilds the log for every day March 2-22 from the source files, computes the training-load values, writes the short report and the memory note, and leaves calories blank for unlogged days.
why: This fails, and the reason is the input materials, not the rubric scoring counts. Of the four photo-like input files, two are genuine phone photos of real notes (crumpled paper, coffee stains, natural handwriting, a desk and pen visible), but the other two - the 'later fixes' note and the 'house rules for the log' note - are clearly digital stock illustrations: flat vector paper on a solid background with an artificial uniform drop shadow, perfectly straight ruled lines with no curl or perspective, and a handwriting font (identical repeated letters, no pen-pressure variation), and the two share the exact same template. That is half the photo inputs looking fake, with no explanation in the task that they are mockups - and these two fake-looking files carry the most important content the rubric grades against (the correction notes and the calorie/spike/recovery house rules). That crosses the line for input realism and is what makes this fail. Separately, there is one small rubric gap: the report is supposed to say what the acute-to-chronic trend says about how sensible the training ramp was, but no criterion checks that conclusion, so a report omitting it would still pass. The numeric values the rubric checks were confirmed correct against the raw exports (the agent's own output ran about 10-12% low), all 10 weights are valid, and several criteria flagged elsewhere were checked and cleared - they each cover one computation or a closed set of dates and are acceptable, and a filename concern about MEMORY.md was dropped because the user later told the agent to write the root MEMORY.md and it did.
fix: Replace the two digital stock-notepad images (the 'later fixes' note and the 'house rules' note) with genuine photos of real handwritten notes, since they carry the corrections and house rules the task depends on; or, if mockups are intentional, say so in the task. Also add a criterion that checks the report actually states what the acute-to-chronic trend implies about how sensible the ramp was.

scenario: For a financial-stewardship small-group session on retirement, the user wants a simple 5-year 401(k) projection built from their own real numbers, but their prep is scattered and they don't fully trust it. They provide a handwritten worksheet photo, a whiteboard snapshot, and a voice memo with fixes, and say to use the real Fidelity figures from their email and the FinTrack records for actual 2025 totals. They include a packet_rules.md that says which source wins, how to do the math, and exactly what each file should contain, and ask the agent to treat it as the rulebook and produce a corrected teaching key, a line-by-line audit CSV, a plain corrections file, a memory log, and - only if something truly can't be pinned down - an open-questions file.
did: A correct response reconciles all the sources following packet_rules.md, produces the named deliverables with the audit CSV in the exact column layout the rulebook specifies, keeps an appended memory log, and only raises an open-questions file for something genuinely unresolvable.

The rulebook (packet_rules.md), which the user says to follow exactly, spells out that packet_audit.csv must have six specific columns in a specific order (item, source, value_as_written, corrected_value, winning_source, status). The rubric only ever checks the corrected_value column - nothing verifies the other five columns or the status values, and the bundled test deliberately leaves column names and order to the rubric. So a response with a differently structured CSV that happens to include a corrected_value column would pass even though it breaks the required layout. Because the CSV is a secondary deliverable, this counts as a small issue, not a serious one. Everything else holds: all 14 weights are valid, both images were viewed and every number was confirmed against the actual records (voice memo, Fidelity, FinTrack, worksheet, whiteboard decoy), and the decoy criteria are correct. The platform's own review claimed a failure on the grounds that five criteria bundle multiple things, but that was overturned - each of those criteria covers a single reconciliation or computation (or a closed, listed set), which is an accepted way to write them, and an automated check agreed there were no real problems with how the criteria are split. Comments about the contributor's rationale text and about a rating on the model's run are out of scope and not counted, and a criterion that only checks the agent's steps is treated as guidance.
fix: Add a criterion that checks packet_audit.csv uses the exact six columns the rulebook requires - item, source, value_as_written, corrected_value, winning_source, status - in that order, rather than only checking the corrected_value column.

She uploads the grid and explains her codes (F+ fine motor, L language, S+ social, I independent), says to use any crossed-out-and-corrected mark instead of the original, to compute FC, LC, SC, IC, and total demonstrated skills for every child, to ignore H and A (help-needed and absent days), and to save the result as Toddler_Development_Observation_Report.md ending with which skill area was strongest across the whole class.

scenario: The user is cleaning up their prep for a new bank-teller privacy lesson and has uploaded rough slide screenshots, a short customer-service audio clip, and messy notes, plus a mention that a colleague (Rachel) sent the official Cascade training documents. They ask the agent to write two files: a study packet for trainees and a trainer-notes file that flags what is confusing or missing in the slides and what still needs checking against the official documents, while being careful not to claim it confirmed anything it could not actually read.

why: This rubric fails, for two reasons that are about the task setup rather than the wording of the criteria. First, the multimedia inputs are not actually needed: a plain-text notes file in the workspace already spells out everything the media contains. It carries a ten-bullet summary of the audio clip, it lists each slide's problems in writing, and it names Rachel's three documents word-for-word, so every request and every content criterion can be satisfied from that text file alone, and the record shows the agent never even opened the audio yet still earned the audio point. The slides and audio can be looked at, but nothing forces the agent to. Second, and relatedly, no criterion (and no real test, since the test file is just a placeholder) is tied to anything you could only get by actually viewing the slide images or hearing the audio, so there is no check that the agent genuinely used the media. On top of these two task-setup problems there is one smaller issue: criterion C6 bundles two separate things into a single pass-or-fail check (which source was consulted for Rachel's documents, and, separately, labeling any document content that could not be confirmed), so an agent that does one but not the other cannot get partial credit.
fix: Remove or rewrite the text notes file so it no longer restates the audio summary, the per-slide problems, and the document names, forcing the agent to actually use the slides and audio. Then add at least one criterion (or a real test) anchored to a detail that can only be obtained by viewing a slide image or listening to the audio, so the rubric verifies the media was genuinely used. Separately, split C6 into two criteria so the source-consulted check and the could-not-confirm labeling check are scored independently.

scenario: A CS 401 instructor recorded session 2 of a counting-and-probability bridge module and saved it with a rules file describing how the write-up should be formatted and a separate note describing what they actually want. They ask the agent to build a corrected solution set, a per-topic mastery summary, and a short cover note for their advisor, told that the lecturer only slipped once (on problem 7, the medical-test one) so the rest can be moved through quickly, with the cover note carrying the advisor's name, title, and phone at the top.
did: A correct response produces the three files following the rules file exactly, including the required column layout and notation, correctly fixes problem 7, confirms the other problems, and writes a mastery summary that marks each topic appropriately.
why: This rubric does not fail, but it has three real problems. First, the rules file explicitly requires a specific way of writing variance (sample versus population), and there is a criterion that checks the combination notation but none that checks the variance notation, so that requirement is not graded at all. Second, the rules file spells out an exact six-column layout for each row plus a one-line reason and a topic column, and no criterion checks that layout, the reason column, or the topic column. Third, one criterion (C19) bundles six separate per-topic mastery judgments into a single pass/fail check, so a response that got some topics right and others wrong (the actual response got two of six right) earns no credit at all instead of partial credit. An earlier review went further and marked this as failing, but two of the items it counted were not valid: one criterion consolidates four similar correct verdicts, which the rules explicitly allow, and another couples a verdict to an answer that is automatically determined by it, so neither is a defect. After removing those, three real problems remain, which moves the result down but not all the way to a failure.
fix: Add a criterion that checks the required variance notation (sample versus population), parallel to the existing combination-notation check. Add a criterion that checks the six-column layout and order plus the reason and topic columns. Split criterion C19 into separate checks for each topic's mastery verdict so partial credit is possible.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A parent rushed out a build sheet for their daughter Emma's school science-fair solar system model and does not trust half of what they wrote. They ask the agent to go through the draft, fix the mistakes, fill in the unfinished parts, and pull everything into one clean build guide saved as solar_system_build_guide.md, without messaging anyone or touching their calendar.
did: A correct response produces a single clean solar_system_build_guide.md with the correct ball sizes for the eight planets, the spoken Saturn correction applied, proper spacing, the due date, no budget figure, and no message or calendar action.
why: This rubric does not fail, but it has one real problem. One criterion (C3) bundles two separate facts into a single pass/fail check: whether the size table lists exactly the eight planets Mercury through Neptune with no Pluto, and separately whether the Sun is treated as a not-to-scale centerpiece rather than a sized ball. A guide could get one of these right and the other wrong, so they should not share one yes/no award. That is a moderate problem. A separate concern about the rubric reaching a failing tally is not valid: it only got there by counting two missing checks (labeling every planet, and a minimum board size) toward failure, but those are secondary teacher rules rather than core requirements, so they are advisory and do not count toward the failing tally. The rest of the build guide's requirements are all covered, and a weight nudge on the Saturn criterion and a note about missing penalty-weighted criteria were both reviewed and found not to be real defects.
fix: Split criterion C3 into two separate checks: one for the size table containing exactly the eight planets with no Pluto, and one for the Sun being a not-to-scale centerpiece. Optionally, you could add explicit criteria for the two secondary teacher rules (label every planet by name, and a board at least 24 by 36 inches) so the guide is graded against them too.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

An earlier review marked this as failing, but the items that pushed it there do not hold up: both output filenames are actually named in the prompt, so there is no missing-filename problem; a criterion penalizing the excluded family's name from leaking into the saved log is a legitimate privacy check, not over-reach; and a batch of empty explanation fields behind several criteria is a form artifact from how the rubric was rebuilt, not a real defect. So one real problem remains, which moves the result down but not to a failure.

scenario: A parent uploaded photos of their daughter Mira's end-of-year school packet (worksheets, a teacher note, and a skills checklist) plus a voicemail from Ms. Chen, and wrote everything they need checked into notes.txt. They ask the agent to follow notes.txt, save it all to mira_progress_review.md, text Theo a short summary before Sunday, and also write to MEMORY.md for later reference.
did: A correct response works through the items in notes.txt using the photos and voicemail, writes the full review to mira_progress_review.md, sends Theo a short summary text, and records the key points in MEMORY.md.
why: This rubric does not fail, though it has a few small issues. One criterion requires a source-by-source consistency analysis covering all four sources (the teacher note, the voicemail, the skills checklist, and the worksheet results) in a single check, so a response that covers three of the four gets no more credit than one that covers none; because the prompt frames cross-source consistency as one synthesis task, this is only a small concern. Another criterion bundles two separable jobs into one statement, mapping the recurring July workshop sessions against the custody weeks and flagging any session on Theo's custody week as a conflict, and a response could reasonably do one without the other. A third criterion is too lenient: it accepts a text to Theo of four sentences or fewer, but the user's notes asked for roughly three sentences max, so a four-sentence message that overshoots the user's guidance still gets credit; this is looseness rather than something that wrongly fails a correct short message. Finally, the user's notes said the text to Theo should give the headline scores and whether they need to do anything, but no criterion checks that the recommendation (the do-we-need-to-act part) is included, so a text with only the scores would pass; this last gap is a minor, peripheral coverage point. Together these add up to only a few small issues, well below the level that would make the rubric fail.
fix: For the all-four-sources criterion, either accept partial source coverage or split it so each source is checked, so a response is not all-or-nothing. Split the workshop-mapping criterion into one check for the session-to-custody mapping and one for flagging conflicts. Tighten the text-length criterion to match the user's roughly-three-sentence guidance, or keep it loose if four is considered acceptable. Add a criterion that checks the text to Theo includes the actionable recommendation (whether they need to do anything), since the user asked for it.
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A crew lead running the monthly safety meeting needed to walk the crew and supervisors through the annual heat-illness refresher. They uploaded this year's training module slides and audio plus today's worksite forecast and pointed the agent at a notes file describing what is in the module and how they want the handout. They asked the agent to build a briefing for today's conditions plus a hydration schedule CSV, a quiz, and flashcards, and to keep changes in a memory file. A later turn corrected the acclimatization method to follow the slide (start at 50%, add 25% per day) and noted there are 7 slides, not 8.
did: A correct response builds the briefing for today's forecast, produces the hydration schedule with the exact required columns, the quiz, and the flashcards, applies the slide's acclimatization method over the voice note where they disagree, and records the voice-note transcript with timestamps and the sources and numbers used in the memory file.
why: This rubric fails review. There are several serious problems. First, one criterion has its scoring backwards: it describes a good behavior (the final message confirms completion and names the files that were created) but attaches a penalty to it, so a correct response that does confirm completion and name its files gets marked down for doing the right thing. Second, the criterion for the hydration schedule is too loose: the prompt requires a CSV with eight specific columns in an exact order, but the criterion accepts any time-based CSV with any columns and nothing else enforces that exact schema. Third, two required parts of the memory file are graded by nothing at all: the prompt asks the memory file to record the voice-note transcript with rough timestamps and to record which sources were used and the numbers landed on, and no criterion (and no test) checks either of these. Together the serious problems add up past the threshold, so the task fails. One platform claim that a key criterion penalized a correct answer was not adopted, because the later turn makes clear the slide method wins, so penalizing the voice-note method is actually a valid check.
fix: Flip the completion-confirmation criterion to a positive reward (or rewrite it to penalize the bad behavior of failing to confirm), so confirming completion and naming the files is credited rather than punished. Tighten the hydration-schedule criterion to require the exact eight columns in the specified order. Add a criterion that checks the memory file records the voice-note transcript with rough timestamps, and another that checks it records the sources used and the numbers landed on.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A father uploads messy photos and papers from his daughter Zoe's school folder and wants help reviewing them gently for homework that night. He asks the agent to look through every file, check them against whatever school context it can find, save a main review packet (zoe_schoolwork_review_packet.md) describing each file and gently explaining the ones that look like Zoe's work, make a gentle 7-day home practice plan, create or update MEMORY.md with only helpful ongoing context, and end the packet with a warm script and a short summary of which files to use, question, or rule out.
did: A correct response reviews each file against Zoe's school context, writes the review packet with gentle per-file explanations and a warm closing script, produces the realistic practice plan, and keeps only the useful ongoing context in MEMORY.md.
why: This rubric fails because it double-scores the same two decisions. There are two pairs of criteria where a positive criterion and a negative criterion reward and penalize the exact same single choice. In the first pair, one criterion gives points for correctly treating two specific image files as too advanced or not Zoe's current work, while another takes points away for putting those same two files in the 'usable' or 'definitely Zoe's' bucket; that is one categorization decision being graded twice. In the second pair, one criterion rewards MEMORY.md recording Zoe's grade as kindergarten and not stating Grade 5, while another penalizes MEMORY.md stating Grade 5 as fact; again, one decision scored from both sides. The underlying facts in all of these are correct, so the criteria are accurate, just redundant. With two of these duplicate-scoring pairs out of thirteen criteria, the rubric crosses the line for serious overlap and fails. An earlier review piled on more findings (disputes over how three criteria were rated and one criterion it called a process check), but those were about whether items were rated correctly rather than flaws in the criteria themselves, and the process-style criterion is only advisory, so they do not add to the count.
fix: Merge or remove the redundant negative criterion in each pair so each decision is scored once. For the file-categorization pair, fold the penalty for misfiling the two advanced files into the single criterion that already rewards classifying them correctly. For the grade pair, fold the penalty for stating Grade 5 into the single criterion that rewards recording kindergarten. Collapsing these two pairs brings the rubric back under the overlap threshold.

scenario: The user is assembling their 11-year-old daughter Chloe's science-fair project for a portfolio and has uploaded her class write-up, original notes, display-board photos, and fair-night pictures, warning that some details may be slightly off because she wrote it from memory. They ask the agent to produce a proper lab report saved as chloe_filtration_lab_report.md and a separate filtration_data.csv holding the pass number, clarity rating, and time for only the trials she actually finished, with all the facts verified.

There are also two smaller wording issues in the report criteria: C8 lumps together a check that all six report sections exist with a vague 'substantive content' requirement that is hard to judge consistently, and C10 bundles three separate header facts (student name, grade, and school) into one pass-or-fail check so partial credit is lost.

For C8, drop the vague 'substantive content' wording and keep a clean check that the six named sections are present. scenario: A runner who finished a 5K kept a handwritten training journal since January and took photos of every page plus a screenshot of their Strava year stats. They asked the agent to go through every journal entry, line it up against their Strava data, finish training_log_reconciled.csv (one row per entry with the date, what it actually was, the real distance, their note copied word-for-word, and a flag where it doesn't match), then write training_summary.md (runs vs walks, real total mileage, longest run, and a 10K-readiness call) and a fresh MEMORY.md.
